The DPA dismissed the complaint because the complainant’s data was deemed ‘generally available’ and the respondent’s processing thereof was justified by their legal mandate to efficiently place workers and provide labour market information.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2022 into ING Bank NV Amsterdam Bucharest Branch, started after the bank notified a personal data breach. Customer data, including identity, contact and banking details and Internet Banking credentials, were accessed and disclosed without authorisation, and third parties made payment operations. The authority found the bank had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of RON 98,076, equal to EUR 20,000, which was paid. The press release also says Raiffeisen Bank SA paid its fine.
The Belgian DPA ordered a Covid-19 contact tracking centre to answer an access request, to which the centre did not reply.
The Romanian DPA fined the President of an Association of Owners €300 for not providing the information requested by the DPA by the legal deadline.

During the COVID-19 emergency in spring 2020, two camera cars were used in Rotterdam to monitor and enforce corona rules, filming public spaces including identifiable adults and children. The police chief had not carried out a data protection impact assessment before the processing began; a pre-assessment concluding none was needed was only adopted on 10 May 2020, and the actual assessment on 26 May 2020, while filming continued. The Dutch DPA found a breach of Article 4c(1) of the Police Data Act. It set a fine of EUR 50,000, reduced from the base amount of EUR 56,500 because of the exceptional crisis circumstances at the start of the pandemic.

The Belgian DPA reprimands a government agency for not proactively involving its DPO in a processing activity relying on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. All processing activities must be in line with the GDPR, even those mandated by legislation predating the GDPR.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in September 2022 at Raiffeisen Bank SA, started after the bank sent 17 personal data breach notifications. Findings included unsigned credit bureau queries, prescoring for an external broker, credits granted to clients who had not requested them, suspected internal fraud, emails with client documents sent to wrong recipients, and disclosure of Smart Mobile account data to other clients. The bank was sanctioned with three fines totalling RON 138,572 (about EUR 28,000) and two warnings, under Articles 32 and 25(1) GDPR.
The Polish DPA fined Virgin Mobile €460,000 for lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures, which resulted in a data breach affecting over 114,000 persons.

The Hungarian DPA fined a news service 2,000,000 HUF (approx. €5,080) for processing personal data without valid consent. Data subjects who signed up for the controller's newsletter were automatically signed up to electronic marketing and a prize draw without being sufficiently informed nor being able to give granular consent.

The Finnish DPA found a healthcare provider to have breached Article 32(1) GDPR and Article 32(2) GDPR for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as encryption, to prevent unauthorised access to personal data.

According to the Slovenian DPA, sending emails containing personal data to unauthorized recipients constitutes unlawful processing under Article 6(1) GDPR. However the authority found a mitigating circumstance since most of the recipients were bound by professional secrecy.

The Finnish DPA held that, according to national law, a parent who is not a legal guardian of the minor child, cannot request rectification or deletion of personal data relating to the child (even if a previous court order had granted him or her access to the inaccurate data).

The French DPA imposed a fine of €800,000 on Discord, an online communication platform. Among other things, the controller had no data retention policy, did not secure the data with a password that was strong enough, and should have conducted a data protection impact assessment.

An 85-year-old woman was called by a call centre in Vodafone's sales network and, she says unknowingly, concluded a fixed-line contract by voice recording. Her son complained to the Garante. The Garante found that Vodafone could not show valid consent to the promotional contact, that the consent formula was undifferentiated and read out too fast to be understood, that no proper information notice was given, and that the contract was presented in breach of fairness and transparency. It banned further processing of the complainant's data and fined Vodafone EUR 500,000, with publication of the decision.

The Garante fined the only health authority of Valle d'Aosta EUR 40,000. During the Covid-19 emergency it had removed the privacy filters on its corporate health dossier by an administrative act, so any health worker could open the dossiers of all patients in the region, whatever their consent or whether they treated them. It also had no measures to detect abnormal access. The case began with a complaint from a health worker who had refused consent to the dossier but whose file was repeatedly accessed by a colleague who had never treated her. The Garante said the Covid rules did not override the general principles and rules for health data in dossiers. This text is a newsletter summary, not the decision itself.

A municipal employee complained that the municipality published on its online notice board, and then in its historical archive, an executive decision containing his name, the amount withheld from his salary for a loan repayment (cessione del quinto), the duration and the bank's IBAN. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis for publishing this data and that the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation were breached. The publication also stayed online beyond the 15-day period because of an automatic archiving function. It fined the municipality EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the dissemination had ended.

A trade union reported that the company, which runs gyms in Milan, had introduced fingerprint-based time clocks for all employees. The Garante asked the company for information twice without any reply, then inspected it in September 2021. It found fingerprint processing of about 132 employees from October 2018 until 2 May 2022, relying on consent in a general employee notice, with minimal information and a processing register that omitted biometric data. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 9, 13 and 30(1)(c) GDPR and of Article 157 of the Code (failure to answer its requests), and fined the company EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

Two people complained that the municipality disclosed excessive personal data (a name, and an identity document) to third parties when handling access-to-records requests, and did not answer their data subject access requests. The Garante also found the municipality had no data protection officer from April 2021 to January 2022. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 12 and 37(1)(a) GDPR. It dropped the charge about failing to notify the first DPO's contact details, treating it as an excusable error. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A man complained that I-Model s.r.l. only formally answered his two erasure requests: it confirmed deletion but kept sending him job-offer SMS messages. The Garante found that the company had given a merely formal reply and kept processing his data without a legal basis after consent was withdrawn. It found violations of Articles 17 and 6(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Two complainants objected that the municipality of Cisterna di Latina disclosed their personal data to third parties (excess data, including an identity document) when handling access-to-documents requests, and did not answer their data subject access requests. It also emerged that the municipality had no data protection officer for several months after the first one resigned. The Garante found breaches of data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)), Art. 12 and Art. 37(1)(a), but closed the complaint about the late communication of the first DPO's contact details as an excusable error. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A student complained that the music conservatory had obtained the recording of an online student assembly, had it transcribed, and used his statements to open disciplinary proceedings against him. The Garante found that the conservatory processed the recording without a valid legal basis and in breach of the principles of lawfulness and purpose limitation. It also found that the conservatory had appointed its Director as data protection officer, which is a conflict of interest. A fine of EUR 6,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A patient complained that at a radiology clinic she was asked to sign on a tablet for privacy without seeing any text, and that no DPO contact details were given. The Garante found the privacy information incomplete (no right to complain, no retention period or criteria, no DPO contact) and that no compliant DPO had been designated. It fined the company EUR 15,000 for breaching Articles 5, 13 and 37 GDPR, ordered it to complete the notice and designate and publish a DPO, and ordered publication of the decision.

The Icelandic DPA rejected the complaint of a data subject based on Article 17 GDPR against Google LLC to remove search results containing their personal data, because their interests were outweighed the right of freedom of expression and information pursuant to Article 17(3)(a) GDPR.
The Icelandic DPA ordered a phone company to introduce appropriate security measures against the accidental reassigning of its costumers phone numbers as required by Article 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA ordered a company to fulfil a data subject's requests. The controller had not responded to an access (Article 15 GDPR) and erasure request (Article 17 GDPR), resulting in violations of Articles 12(3), 15(1) and 17(1) GDPR.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint concerning unwanted marketing e-mails. The GDPR was not applicable because the controller did not have any establishments in the EEA (Article 3(1) GDPR), there was no offering of goods and services to data subjects in the EEA (Article 3(2)(a) GPDR) nor did any monitoring of EU-based individuals take place (Article 3(2)(b) GDPR).

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board upheld a decision of the Norwegian DPA to reject a complaint due to lack of competence under Article 57(1)(a) GDPR. The complaint concerned lawfulness of personal data processing and access to records from the Child Welfare Service.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation in October 2022 into a company that published on its website 23 named decisions terminating employment contracts of people with no legal relationship to it. These contained names, positions, contract numbers and disciplinary offences. The company could not show a lawful basis for the online disclosure. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 6 GDPR, fined the company RON 24,683.5 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered removal or anonymisation of identifying information.

The Belgian DPA warned a controller for publishing an invoice with personal data on Facebook. The controller did not have a legal basis (Article 6 GDPR) and did not delete the invoice after the data subject requested erasure.

The Belgian DPA warned an employer and ordered it to comply with an erasure request of a former employee. The controller's website contained pictures and the former position of the data subject, more than 6 months after her dismissal.
The Polish DPA fined a municipality €1,700 for not taking adequate measures to prevent a security breach, which resulted in compromising the confidentiality of 51 sets of personal data.

The Portuguese DPA reprimanded and fined the municipality of Setubal €170,000 for violations of the integrity and confidentiality principle, the storage limitation principle, the information obligations from Article 13 GDPR and for not appointing a DPO with regard to the collection of personal data of Ukrainian refugees, who were using a helpline in Portugal.
The Greek DPA examined the Ministry of Education and Religious Affairs compliance with the provisions of the legislation on the processing of personal data with regards to distant learning.

The Icelandic DPA ordered a car repair shop to comply with an Article 15 GDPR access request by providing a data subject with data of all repairs and services done to his car while it was in his possession.
The Spanish Data Protection agency held that the sending of an email regarding personal data to a not authorised recipient infringes Articles 5 and 32 GDPR.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a controller for a cookie banner that did not comply with Articles 6 and 4(11) GDPR as the consent was not informed and because the controller used colours and designs to influence the user's choice in violation of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.
The Authority, acting unanimously, shall decide to specify the rules for the removal of identification in its decisions posted on its website.

A person reported receiving by certified email the histology report of another patient, sent by mistake by the Careggi hospital in Florence. Careggi acted as processor for I.S.P.R.O., the controller and the regional oncology institute. The Garante found that I.S.P.R.O., as controller, remained responsible and should have supervised its processor. It declared the processing unlawful for breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and fined I.S.P.R.O. EUR 7,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective orders were imposed as measures against recurrence had been implemented.

A complainant, a lawyer employed by the Fondazione Teatro Regio di Torino, objected that the foundation had published on its 'transparent administration' web page three decisions containing her personal data, including sick certificates and a reference to a precautionary suspension. The Garante found that the foundation had published health data, whose dissemination is expressly prohibited, and information not necessary for the purpose, without a legal basis. It treated the fault as negligent and isolated and took into account the data being blacked out, staff training and cooperation. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

A person complained that the Careggi hospital trust sent him by certified email another patient's histological report. The trust acts as processor for ISPRO in this lab activity; a clerk attached the wrong report from a spool folder holding two near-identical names. The Garante found a breach of the confidentiality principle, of Article 9 and of the security obligations in Article 32. It fined the trust EUR 9,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but imposed no corrective orders because the trust had already changed its procedure.

On 20 October 2022, the Italian Data Protection Authority issued an injunction against a Higher Education Institute, imposing an administrative penalty of €900, for publishing the personal data of one of its employees on its institutional website.

The Italian Archery Federation published on its website a disciplinary decision against the complainant. It contained data on criminal convictions and offences and stayed online for about five years. The Garante found no suitable legal basis for publishing it. The federation's reliance on the transparency decree was rejected. The Garante also found the five-year retention unjustified and breaches of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation and storage limitation. It fined the federation EUR 10,000. No further corrective measures were ordered, because the federation had already redacted the data and de-indexed the pages after the complaint.

A resident complained that the municipality used video surveillance during the COVID-19 lockdown to detect a lockdown breach, had inadequate signage, and ignored his request for access to the footage. The Garante found the municipality's signage and full privacy notice inadequate, no retention period fixed for images used for administrative purposes, a fee wrongly demanded for access, and no record of processing activities for a period. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the municipality EUR 12,000, ordered it to provide the footage free of charge (or justify refusal) within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A customer complained that Douglas Italia did not answer her data subject request. The Garante then inspected the company in late 2021 and examined its marketing and profiling processing. It found that the app collected a bundled consent that was neither free nor specific, that the company could not document consents or notices inherited from three merged companies, that the data of about 3.3 million inactive customers were kept without justification, that the privacy notice was incomplete, and that telemarketing by stores lacked procedures. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures and deletion of old data, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,400,000, publishing the decision.
The Italian DPA imposed a €30,000 fine on a clinic for having requested Covid passes before entering the clinic’s premises without a proper legal basis.

After auditing the Norwegian Directorate of Correctional Service for 1,5 years, the DPA ordered it to sort out and document its controller responsibilities and update internal controls for managing privacy and personal data protection throughout the organisation.

The UK DPA imposed a fine of around €5,100,000 (GBP 4,400,000) on the controller for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure employee's personal data, which contributed to a data breach caused by a cyberattack, contrary to Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that a bank was not the controller of personal information communicated through its employees' office emails pursuant to Article 4(7) GDPR when the emails did not concern the bank's activities.

The Belgium DPA held that a social housing organisation could rely on Article 6(1)(e) GDPR to investigate foreign assets of data subjects and on Article 49(1)(d) GDPR for international data transfers in connection with this purpose. However, the DPA reprimanded the controller for violations of Articles 28(2) and 28(3) GDPR in a data processing agreement.

The Belgian DPA ordered a controller, a vacation park owner, to comply with the principle of data minimisation pursuant to Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. The controller legally processed personal data according to Article 6(1)(b) GDPR to prevent the fraudulent abuse of a swimming pool discount card, but unnecessarily requested photos and degree of kinship of the data subject's family members when their names alone would have sufficed.
The French DPA fined a controller €20,000,000 under Article 83 GDPR for violating Articles 6, 12, 15, 17 and 32 GDPR by providing a facial recognition service.
The DPA classifies a case without follow-up because the grievance is part of a broader dispute which can be more effectively solved through other legal remedies.
The Belgian DPA warned a controller for a violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by requiring the data subject to provide the copy of an ID card to exercise their right of erasure under Article 17 GDPR.
The Belgian DPA ordered an employer to process an access request from its employee even though the employer claimed to have never received the request.

In an Article 60 GDPR decision, the Swedish DPA reprimanded a company for, among others, a violation of Article 6 GDPR. Since the data subject had provided an invalid e-mail address for the order confirmation, the company, in an attempt to track the client, shared his data with the e-mail domain provider.

A user complained that the online user area of a water utility's website, which handled logins, contact details and invoices, ran over unencrypted http with no SSL certificate. The Garante's own check confirmed it. The utility moved to https after the proceedings began and cooperated. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25(1) and 32 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ended.

The Italian DPA opened an ex officio investigation into the Clubhouse voice social network after press reports, later also receiving a report. The US operator, which has no EU establishment, argued Italy had no jurisdiction but the Garante found the GDPR applicable because the service was offered to people in the EU. It found unlawful processing, including lack of a valid legal basis, transparency and information failings, an inadequate EU representative, missing processor appointments, inadequate security and no data protection impact assessment. It fined the company EUR 2,000,000, ordered corrective measures, banned further direct marketing, profiling and account-information sharing, and ordered publication of the decision.

A volunteer member of a social cooperative resigned and asked in the same letter for his personal data to be erased. The cooperative acknowledged the resignation but did not answer the erasure request within one month, and gave no reasons or information about complaint rights until the Garante intervened. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in relation to Article 17 GDPR and fined the cooperative EUR 10,000. It also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A woman, as heir of two deceased relatives, complained that Poste Italiane did not answer her access request. Poste admitted a clerical error by an employee delayed the handling of the request; it replied only in January 2022, after requesting documents proving her heir status. The Garante found that Poste breached Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR by not answering within one month nor informing her of the reasons and remedies. It fined Poste EUR 10,000, noting negligence, cooperation and no previous violations. No further order was needed since the access request had been satisfied.

The Italian DPA fined the Veneto Region €100,000 for disclosing the data of 12,580 non-vaccinated health workers outside the regulatory framework provided for by national law, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR.
The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint for reasons of expediency, since the lack of evidence would require disproportionate resources for the investigation compared to the importance of the complaint.

The UK DPA imposed a fine of 1,350,000 GBP on a catalogue retailer for violating Articles 9 and 13 GDPR by profiling special category (health) data of their customers based on their product purchases without acquiring consent or informing them about it.

Following its earlier Decision 48/2018 on contactless cards, the Authority checked whether Alpha Bank had informed customers that the chip of older Mastercard debit/credit cards stores a history of recent transactions readable contactlessly. The bank had not informed customers and instead chose to phase out the feature by replacing cards. The Authority found a violation of Article 13 GDPR, considering it deliberate, continuing and affecting a large number of customers. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000.

Following earlier Decision 48/2018 on contactless cards, the Greek DPA checked whether Eurobank had complied with its recommendation to inform cardholders that the chip of older Mastercard cards stores the date and amount of recent transactions, readable contactlessly. The check was prompted by a customer's request. The Authority found that Eurobank had not informed customers and had instead decided to phase out the processing by replacing cards. It found a breach of the Article 13 GDPR information obligation and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000.

Following earlier complaints about contactless cards, the Authority had in Decision 48/2018 recommended that banks inform customers when their cards keep a history of recent transactions in the chip, readable contactlessly. Piraeus Bank did not inform its customers and instead began gradually replacing cards with the feature deactivated, saying notification would be costly and unnecessary. The Authority found a breach of the information duty in Article 13 GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000 under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(5) GDPR.

The Authority examined whether National Bank of Greece had complied with its Decision 48/2018, which recommended informing cardholders that their cards kept a history of recent transactions on the chip, readable contactlessly. It found that the bank had not informed customers about this processing and had instead chosen to phase it out by replacing cards. The Authority found a breach of Article 13 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 under Article 58(2)(i) in conjunction with Article 83(5).

Spanish DPA held a controller responsible for a data breach since they did not have sufficient measures in place to avoid data breaches. Although some measures were applied, they did not provide an adequate level of protection for sensitive data.

The Belgian DPA held that, pursuant to Article 16 GDPR, a controller had to comply with a rectification request concerning incorrect contact information which prevented the data subject from receiving his daughter's progress reports.
The Belgian DPA gave a controller a warning for violating Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), 5(1)(c), 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR by recording the private space of its neighbours with a security camera.

When the controller refused to provide access to the freeze frame data of a vehicle (a type of component reading) to the data subject, the Belgian DPA held that the controller had to provide an answer to the request within 14 days.
The Belgian DPA used Article 58(2)(c) GDPR to order a controller to comply with an erasure request of a data subject pursuant to Article 17 GDPR after it failed to reply to the initial request.

The Hungarian DPA fined a media provider 10,000,000 HUF (approx. €25,650) for, among other things, failing to properly inform data subjects about the processing on its websites and for confusingly using the term "legitimate interest" without referring to its meaning under the GDPR.

The Belgian DPA held that a controller, with companies in both Belgium and the UK, violated Article 15(1) GDPR, Article 15(3) GDPR and Article 12(3) GDPR GDPR for deleting data instead of providing access to data after an access request by the data subject.

The DPA of Cyprus fined the Cyprus electricity authority €5,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 24(1) and 32 GPDR for delivering a consent form containing personal data to the data subject's neighbour, resulting in an unauthorized disclosure of personal data to a third party.

A landowner in a new development area received a purchase offer for his plot from a property developer, with no information on where the developer got his data. The authority found that a surveying engineer used his access to the electronic land register to identify several hundred owners in two cases and passed the data to the developer. The developer wrote to them without the Article 14 information. The authority fined the developer EUR 50,000 and the surveying engineer EUR 5,000 for unlawful collection and disclosure and breach of information duties. Both accepted the fines and they are final.

Following two personal data breach notifications from the controller, the Romanian authority investigated a publisher. One breach was a customer database file posted on a public forum; the other was a ransomware attack affecting about 100 employees and collaborators. The authority found the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the controller 24,566 lei (about EUR 5,000) under Article 32 GDPR and ordered it to review and update its security measures.

The Icelandic DPA held that a school violated Article 5(1)(d) GDPR by processing incorrect information about the attendance of a child. However, since the inaccuracies were rectified within 12 hours, no further actions were necessary.

The Berlin data protection authority fined a subsidiary of a Berlin e-commerce group EUR 525,000 because its data protection officer had a conflict of interest. He was also managing director of two group service companies that process personal data on behalf of the company he was supposed to supervise. The authority had issued a warning in 2021, and a later check showed the situation continued, so it imposed the fine. The fine was not yet final at the time of the press release.

A mother complained that the Rieti local health authority had sent her daughter, who died in 1995, an invitation to a cervical cancer screening programme. The Garante found that the regional screening database (SIPSOweb), run by Lazio Region, held outdated data, and that the Region had not correctly identified the roles of the parties involved, the legal bases for the processing, or the information to give to data subjects. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered the Region to correct roles, purposes, legal bases and information notices within 90 days, and fined it EUR 100,000. The decision is also to be published on the Garante's website.
The Italian DPA deemed a sign featuring a figure of a stylised camera insufficient to inform about the use of CCTV cameras and fined the controller €2,000.

A former job candidate and employee complained that the bank did not answer his erasure requests on time or properly. His January 2019 request was never actioned because of an internal mishap, and the reply to his lawyer's later requests came only on 17 June 2019, about four months after the legal deadline. The bank also failed to tell him he could complain to the authority or go to court when it declined to erase data it lawfully kept. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in connection with Article 17 and fined the bank EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.
The Italian DPA imposed a €3,000 fine on a municipality for publishing on a public notice board a matriculation number, which allowed for the identification of the data subject.

An employee complained that FCA Italy never answered his formal access request of January 2021 for the data in his personnel file and related work records. The company said it intended to reply in a face-to-face meeting that was repeatedly postponed, and that much of the data was already available to him through an intranet platform and a phone service. The Garante held that the company should have replied in writing within the legal deadline, and that data already held by the person can still be requested. It found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 40,000, taking into account a previous similar finding against it.
The Irish DPA found Airbnb Ireland UC’s request for photo ID, in order to process a data subject’s erasure request, to be unlawful.

The French DPA fined a company €250,000 for infringing Article 5(1)(e) GDPR. It violated the provision by storing personal data for an excessive period of time and by lacking adequate security as passwords were stored without encryption and sent in plain text by email.

The Swedish DPA reprimanded a controller for violating Article 9 GDPR by publishing sensitive data in its background check database, such as information about compulsory care due to mental illness and addiction.

The Hungarian DPA fined a company €73,500 for using consent as general authorization to use personal data for any purposes and for failing to properly inform data subjects about separate processing purposes, including Google and Facebook advertisements.

In a surveillance camera case, the Spanish DPA considered that installing a security camera that also captured the private garden of their neighbour was not be justified by security reasons, and was not proportionate.

The Authority examined a video surveillance system at a private school after complaints from teachers who said they were filmed in classrooms without being informed or consenting. The school said the cameras covered yards, balconies and an events hall, did not record, and that it kept no records of processing activities. The Authority found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, transparency, purpose limitation and accountability, and of Articles 6, 12, 13 and 30 GDPR. It ordered the cameras to be uninstalled within one month and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. Negligence and cooperation were treated as mitigating; the fact that children were affected was noted.

The Danish DPA ordered Aarhus municipality, amongst other things, to change their data processing agreement with Google and bring all third country transfers in line with the GDPR, following the DPA's most recent Helsingor decision.

The Romanian authority opened an investigation on its own initiative after online reports of a possible data breach at Realmedia Network SA, operator of the imobiliare.ro property platform. It found that a service used to run the platform had suffered a security breach exposing the personal data of 194,309 people, including ID copies and personal numeric codes. The company had not put in place technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk. It was fined 39,272 lei, about EUR 8,000, for breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that the processing of personal data for a gene research project was in line with the GDPR because, among other things, it is possible to author a scientific article without being the controller of the analysed personal data.

The Spanish DPA denied a complaint about the surveillance camera pointing to a sidewalk in front of a private parking lot, as it was considered an essential surface to protect people and property, not being demonstrated the processing of any personal data.

The Austrian DPA held that a controller may not lodge a complaint against itself as one of the necessary preconditions to the right to complaint, pursuant to Article 77(1) GDPR, is to be personally affected by the processing of personal data.

Due to a technical error it is here, we apologize for any inconvenience</big> The Polish DPA fined a cultural organisation €529 for not concluding a written agreement under Article 28 GDPR with its processor.

The Spanish DPA has obliged a dental clinic to respond, in ten days, a patient who had requested his clinical records without receiving any answer, as it was considered a legitimate exercise of his right to access.

The Danish DPA held that a political party had a sufficient legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR to investigate its member for alleged sexual violence. However, it reprimanded the controller and processor for not informing the data subject about the processing as required by Article 14(2)(b) GDPR.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the Agency of Family Law (a public authority) for 37 data breaches due to the accidental sharing of protected information about one party to a proceeding with another party, in violation of Article 32(1) GDPR.

The journalists' insurance fund EDOEAP used the ZEUS platform of EDYTE SA, as its processor, for an electronic board election. After the vote, three losing candidates obtained a prosecutor's order and asked EDYTE for voter data. EDYTE handed over the data of about 4,500 voters (names, emails, IP addresses, tax numbers used as voter IDs). It did so despite the controller's express objection, and the voters were not informed beforehand. The Authority found there was no express legal obligation, since the data were private documents and the order was not binding outside criminal proceedings. It held that EDYTE had acted contrary to Article 29 GDPR and so became an independent controller under Article 28(10), which it breached. It fined EDYTE EUR 5,000.

The EDPB adopted a binding decision, following which the Irish DPC fined Meta €405,000,000 for the lack of legal grounds for processing contact information on children’s business accounts and ‘public by default’-settings for child users.
The DPA held that the controller rightfully deleted the data subject's information after finding out that the data subject was a minor in the context of an access request.

A school employee complained that the school published on its website and on the CLASSEVIVA electronic register a circular on summer leave with an attachment showing, next to names, the code "104" (benefits under Law 104/1992), which reveals health information. The school admitted it was a material error and removed the document. The Garante found unlawful processing (dissemination on the website and communication to all staff in the reserved area) in breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and the Italian Code provisions. It imposed a fine of EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Danish DPA determined that a game developer did not have to provide anti-cheat information to a gamer who had filed an access request. The DPA also determined that the game developer only had to provide a copy of in-game chat messages that were sent directly to, and by, the data subject. It did not have to disclose other in-game chat messages, pursuant to Article 15(4) GDPR.
A controller was fined €1,200 by the DPA for failing to have a privacy policy available on a number of webpages despite collecting the personal data of website visitors, violating Article 13 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA notified a bank as a controller, ABANCA, for not replying to a data subject's exercise right, violating Article 12 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA denied a complaint regarding an e-mail sent from a businessman to his ex-wife, with a copy to the counselor of the school where their son studies, informing the existence of a criminal proceeding against her, as it was seen as a private matter.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a processor for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by not testing a new system functionality sufficiently, which led to foster parents gaining access to information about foster children.
The Norwegian DPA fined a company €20,000 for an unlawful credit rating of an incorrect person with a similar name to their customer, and instructed them to implement new routines for credit ratings.

A project manager at Recover AS ran a credit check on a woman who had no customer relationship with the company. The manager had searched Google for the invoice address of a new customer, and the complainant had almost the same name as that customer. Datatilsynet found that the company had no legal basis for the credit check under Article 6(1)(f) and that its credit-check procedure was too general to meet Article 24. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 200,000 and ordered the company to improve its internal control and routines for credit checks.

The Hungarian DPA reprimanded a public body responsible for child protection for obstructing the exercise of the right of access to an audio recording containing the data subject’s voice in violation of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR.

An individual secretly installed a hidden WiFi camera inside a public toilet cubicle on three days between June and July 2020 and recorded users without their knowledge. The Austrian DSB found unlawful processing without a legal basis (Art. 5(1)(a), (b), (c), Art. 6(1)(f)) and a failure to inform data subjects (Art. 5(1)(a) with Arts. 12 and 13). It rejected the household exemption because the camera covered a public space and found intentional conduct. It imposed a single fine of EUR 25,000 (with 336 hours substitute imprisonment) plus EUR 2,500 procedural costs, relying on general prevention and the offender's income and assets.
The Finnish DPA issued a warning to a controller for possible automated individual decision-making related to the assessment of health benefits in violation of Article 22 GDPR.

After an investigation completed in July 2022, the Romanian authority found that Enel Energie Muntenia had emailed a reply containing another customer's visible personal data and documents to a complainant. The controller gave no clear explanation of the error, no evidence of remedial measures and no proof it notified the breach. It was fined RON 49,337 (about EUR 10,000) under Article 32 and given a warning under Article 33. Corrective orders under Article 58(2)(d) require better security measures, contacting the complainant to have the data deleted, and internal measures to prevent recurrence.

Following the EDPB's binding decision under Article 65(1)(a) GDPR, the French DPA increased its fine to Accor hotels from €100,000 to €600,000, notably for direct marketing without valid consent, not respecting GDPR rights of its customers and using weak passwords, in violation of Articles 12, 13, 15, 21 and 32 GDPR.

A patient complained that a medical laboratory's online results portal (Cyberlab), used by doctors to view health analysis results, ran over unencrypted http, and that no DPIA had been done and information was lacking. The Inspection Service confirmed this; the laboratory only introduced TLS 1.2 after the inspection contacted it. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of integrity and confidentiality, security, transparency and DPIA obligations. It fined the laboratory EUR 20,000 (reduced from a proposed EUR 25,000 because of its financial losses) and dismissed the remaining findings.

The Finnish DPA reprimanded a healthcare provider for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of personal data processing in the electronic healthcare appointment booking system.
The Latvian DPA issued a reprimand against a police office for not having established appropriate data processing procedures to deal with a domestic violence case.

The Spanish DPA held that Google LLC was under a legal obligation to preserve search results relating to an employee selection process at a public body and rightfully rejected a data subject's request to de-index the search results relating to their name.

The Spanish DPA imposed a €5,000 fine on a real-state agency for violating Article 13 GDPR because the contract for the purchase of property did not include a clause informing the customer how her personal data gathered in that contract was handled.

The Danish DPA proposed a €6,700 fine against a municipality for not preventing its employees from manually disabling access codes on their mobile phones that contained citizens' personal data, thereby exposing them to unnecessary risk. The police will investigate the case before a final decision is made in the courts.

The Hungarian authority investigated, on its own initiative after several complaints, Amplifon Hungary's postal mailings inviting people to hearing screenings under the label of 'market research'. It found the company used names and addresses obtained from the Interior Ministry register without proper information, a specific genuine purpose or a legal basis. It found breaches of fairness, purpose limitation, Art. 6(1) and the information duties of Arts. 12(1) and 14. It ordered deletion of the stored name and address data and imposed a fine of HUF 80,000,000.

The Hungarian DPA imposed a €200,000 fine on Amplifon for sending direct marketing letters. The company mislead approximately 3-400.000 data subjects about the purposes of processing and unlawfully used consent as a legal basis.

In an Article 60 GDPR decision, the Berlin DPA reprimanded a controller for the violation of Articles 6, 12(3) and 17 GDPR. In order to comply with an erasure request, the controller requested the data subject to log in with her customer account, which she did not have, because she was never a customer.
The Danish DPA reprimanded an e-commerce platform for violating Article 17(1)(c) GDPR by not complying with an erasure request. The DPA ordered the platform to comply.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in June 2022 into a transport company after a complaint that its website gave no information on how personal data is collected, on data subject rights or on breach notification. The company did not supply the information the authority asked for within the legal deadline, breaching Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR, and it did not give clear and complete information to data subjects, breaching Article 12(1). It was fined 34,630.40 lei (about EUR 7,000) for the Article 58 breach and received a warning for the Article 12(1) breach. It was also ordered to give data subjects all the information required by Article 12 in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form.

The Hungarian DPA held that the National Health Insurance Fund's organisational deficiencies and lack of human resources during the COVID-19 pandemic caused an Article 12 GDPR infringement as the controller failed to provide transparent information to a large number of data subjects.

The Danish DPA found that a fitness centre did not violate the GDPR by using video surveillance on its premises. However, the DPA reprimanded the fitness centre for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by storing its employees' data on a shared computer.

The Authority examined, on its own initiative, the processing of personal data when COVID-19 self-test results were declared on the self-testing.gov.gr platform under several joint ministerial decisions. It found that IDIKA kept data longer than the law allowed, breaching the storage limitation principle because it had not taken appropriate measures under Article 25, and fined it EUR 5,000. It also fined the Ministry of Interior and the Naval Pension Fund EUR 5,000 each for failing to carry out a data protection impact assessment. It reprimanded several controllers for incomplete information under Article 13 and for Article 35 failings, and ordered the Naval Pension Fund to remove its application and delete data. Two members dissented and would have imposed only a reprimand.

The Hungarian DPA ruled that an audio recording during installation works is unlawful because it violated the principles of purpose limitation, data minimisation, and did not appropriately inform the data subjects. The controller was fined €700.

A man complained that Cosmopol Security did not answer his access request after he received invoices from a company he had no contract with. The company had bought a business unit from another firm and never properly informed the transferred customers about the change of controller. It had deleted the complainant's data without replying to him. The Garante found breaches of the rules on responding to data subject requests, on information to be given when data is not collected from the person, and on access. It ordered the company to reply to the complainant within 30 days and fined it EUR 20,000.

The Italian DPA fined a controller €1,000 for sending promotional messages without the data subject's consent and for ineffectively monitoring the third party carrying out the processing in its interest.

The District Court of Munich dismissed a data subject's claims for damages pursuant to Article 32(1) and 82(1) GDPR. The data subject had sought damages for the insufficient security measures of a costumer loyalty programme. However, the security standard was deemed high enough pursuant to national law.

A patient complained that a diagnostic centre could not give her copies of the images from a 2018 digital mammography. The centre had lost the images, which were stored on a hard-disk (NAS) system it could only partly recover. The Authority rejected the access-right complaint because the data was already unavailable, but examined security of processing on its own initiative. It found a breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f)) read with Art. 32 and fined the centre EUR 30,000. It also reprimanded the centre for late breach notification under Art. 33 and ordered it to tell the affected data subjects of the breach under Art. 34.

Datatilsynet fined a company NOK 300,000 for carrying out two credit assessments on two people who had no customer relationship or other connection to it. The complaint came from those two people. The authority found that the company had no legal basis and no legitimate interest in running the checks. It also ordered the company to write written routines for credit assessments. This is a press release, not the full decision.

The Italian DPA ruled that outdated information on surveillance cameras' signs breaches the principle of lawful, fair, and transparent processing. It also held that a DPO of an entity cannot act simultaneously as defense counsel for the same entity.

The Belgian DPA held that a controller can rely on legitimate interest as a legal basis to send former customers direct marketing if the relationship ended 'not that long ago' and the data subject did not object to this processing.
The CNIL decided to close a complaint related to the right to erasure following the measures taken by the controller to prevent this situation from arising again.

The Lower Saxony data protection authority fined Volkswagen AG EUR 1.1 million over research drives testing a driver assistance system. A test vehicle recording surrounding traffic was stopped by Austrian police in 2019. The authority found four low-severity violations: missing camera information signs (Art. 13), no processor agreement with the service provider running the drives (Art. 28), no data protection impact assessment (Art. 35) and incomplete documentation in the record of processing activities (Art. 30). Volkswagen cooperated, fixed the defects promptly and accepted the fine notice. The research drives themselves were not objected to.

The Swedish DPA reprimanded Google LLC for refusing several requests for search results' removal under Article 17(1) and 21 GDPR. The DPA held that Google could not refuse to assess the continuing relevance and accuracy of the concerned web pages' contents just because they were behind a paywall.

The Municipal Misdemeanor Court in Zagreb ruled that municipal wardens have a valid legal basis under Article 6 GDPR to collect and process vehicle registration numbers. The legal basis is a statutory obligation prescribed by Article 229 of the Act on Road Traffic Safety.

The Greek DPA partially revoked its previous decision and reduced the fine from €20,000 to €5,000 on a company that sells sports clothing in light of new evidence revealing that the violation of the right to object was due to an isolated error and not to malicious intent.

The Luxembourg DPA fined a bank institution €10,000 for using surveillance cameras without sufficiently informing the data subjects and filming some of them continuously. The above was in breach of Article 5(1)(c) and Article 13 GDPR.

The DPA held that a payment service can process information on the items purchased by a customer from an online pharmacy and an online sex shop based on its legitimate interest to minimise mid-transaction payment cancellations and for fraud prevention purposes. Furthermore, the DPA held that the specific information on purchased items was not sensitive data.

A press release from the Croatian DPA announces two administrative fines. The one matching this record concerns a car sales and service centre in Zagreb. During an unannounced ex officio inspection the Agency found that rooms and outside areas under video surveillance were not marked as such, contrary to Article 27(1) of the Croatian GDPR Implementation Act. It imposed a fine of 30 thousand kuna. The other fine in the release (2.15 million kuna against a telecom provider for security failings) is a different case.
